Unfortunately, it's not that simple. Mars lacks a hot rotating core. It does not produce a strong enough magnetic field to help repel solar radiation. As a result, any atmosphere we put on mars will get bombarded by solar winds and literally blown away from the planet.

Another (and in my opinion, far worse) problem with mars is the relatively low gravity in comparison with earth. Animals with endoskeletons like us evolved bone replacement mechanisms suitable for earth's gravity, but unsuitable for micro-gravity environments.

A better candidate for colonization is, surprisingly, Venus. The caveat is that colonizing Venus requires floating habitats high enough in the atmosphere to be safe. This may actually be possible to overcome since a balloon filled with breathable earth-like air would float in the Venusian atmosphere.

Unlike Mars, Venus has a strong magnetic field and a protective atmosphere similar to earth's at the higher altitudes currently being proposed. Venus' gravity is also much closer to earth's at 0.9 Gs. A level of gravity that has been hypothesized to be of no significant detriment to human skeletal structure.

It appears as though you have a...ahem... Romantic view of what the Roman senate was.

Although cited as the model of our democracy, the Roman senate was, initially, an assembly of representatives from strictly the ruling class- the patricians- and representative of only the interests of their respective families. Not the interests of the common folk. During both the kingdom of Rome and the Republic, senators were often chosen from these patrician clans by either the king or the consuls which were akin to an executive branch after the republic was established (republic in the sense that it was lacking a monarch, not in the common connotation of representative democracy).

The "everyone else", the plebeians, had to wrest political control through other branches of the Roman government, i.e. the consuls, because the Senate was not elected by or for them. Caesar's populism and hard lines against the senate is what made him popular amongst the people during the civil wars.

The senate was, especially with it's nigh hereditary aspects, more akin to something like a council of lords in a feudalistic monarchy.

  4. We, as a populace, are far too reactionary. I could see a lot of swing back and forth, with drastic consequences.
